facts.text: FMVSS 127 is the United States rule requiring automatic emergency braking on new cars; NHTSA writes such rules and investigates defects, NTSB independently investigates accidents, and IIHS is an insurer-funded institute that tests and rates vehicles.
facts.quote: FMVSS 127 is the United States rule requiring automatic emergency braking on new cars, NHTSA is the agency that writes such rules and investigates defects, NTSB is the independent board that investigates accidents, and IIHS is the insurer-funded institute that tests and rates vehicles.

facts.text: United States road-vehicle safety rules are Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards written by NHTSA; manufacturers self-certify compliance and NHTSA checks afterward.
facts.quote: road-vehicle safety rules are Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards (FMVSS), written by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA); manufacturers self-certify to them and NHTSA checks afterward.

facts.text: FMVSS 127 covers automatic emergency braking for light vehicles up to 4,536 kg.
facts.quote: FMVSS No. 127 is the automatic emergency braking (AEB) rule for light vehicles up to 4,536 kg

facts.text: The FMVSS 127 final rule was issued on 9 May 2024, with compliance from 1 September 2029.
facts.quote: final rule 9 May 2024, compliance from 1 September 2029.

facts.text: FMVSS 127 requires no-contact avoidance of a lead vehicle up to 62 mph, pedestrian AEB in daylight and darkness, and forward-collision warning.
facts.quote: It requires no-contact avoidance of a lead vehicle up to 62 mph, pedestrian AEB in daylight and darkness, and forward-collision warning

facts.text: FMVSS 127 specifies two false-activation tests: a steel trench plate at 80 km/h and a pass-through between parked vehicles.
facts.quote: with two false-activation tests, a steel trench plate at 80 km/h and a pass-through between parked vehicles

facts.text: FMVSS 127 false-activation tests fail if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more.
facts.quote: failing if peak deceleration exceeds manual braking by 0.25 g or more

facts.text: Car makers petitioned against FMVSS 127 citing false-activation risk and sued in January 2025.
